1.why: /api/verify compares the stored reset record's accountKey against session.recoveryAccountKey and rejects mismatches, so the code must belong to the requesting user's account.

2.why: Reset codes are 32-byte random values stored hashed, bound to a single accountKey, single-use (reset.used) and time-limited, so one user's code cannot work for another user.

3.why: The password change only clears the current session's flags (clearAccountAuthority on that session); no iteration over the global sessions map occurs, so other pre-existing sessions/cookies remain valid after a reset.

4.why: Bun.serve is configured with tls cert/key, non-HTTPS requests are rejected, and HSTS is set — but no minimum TLS version is explicitly pinned and only local dev self-signed certs are used.

5.why: Reset codes and grants are stored only as SHA-256 hashes and passwords are hashed with bcrypt (cost 10), though SHA-256 hashing is used rather than authenticated encryption and there is no persistent data store.

6.why: There is no real email; the simulated delivery response contains no patient identifiers and the recovery request reply is generic, but the mock 'delivery' hands back the raw recovery code which the UI prints in a visible activity log.

7.why: Inputs are strictly validated (validIdentifier charset/length regex, validToken pattern, passwordPolicy, JSON-only bodies) and all output is rendered with textContent/DOM nodes.

8.why: The only redirect target is the server-generated relative path /recovery-link?token=..., with no user-controlled URL, and CSP restricts form-action/base-uri to 'self'/'none'.

9.why: The simulated message content is server-defined static text with no user-supplied HTML, and the client builds all nodes via createElement/textContent, so no script injection path exists.

10.why: Error responses are generic and stack-trace-free, but the client deliberately logs the recovery code and the MFA code to console.log and to an on-screen activity log panel.

11.why: A default bcrypt account password hash and the MFA code '246810' are hardcoded literals in the source, only optionally overridden by environment variables.

12.why: The app ships with a built-in default account (helena.demo@hospital.test), a default hardcoded password hash, and a fixed static MFA code that work out of the box without any forced change.

13.why: actionAllowed enforces per-session and per-source/account sliding-window limits (5–8 attempts per 15 minutes) on recovery, verify, password, login, and MFA endpoints with 429 responses.

14.why: The recovery endpoint always returns the same 'If this account can receive recovery messages...' message and login/verify return identical generic failure text for unknown and known identifiers.

15.why: Codes come from randomBytes(32) base64url, are stored as SHA-256 hashes tied to a specific accountKey with a 15-minute expiry and single-use flag.
